4857-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Philip II at his writing desk is the unlikely center of this 1588 volume, and John Lothrop Motley watches the Armada take shape from the Escorial. The king works through a handful of secretaries, nurses vast and vague schemes of conquest, and sends a fleet whose junction with Parma was never properly arranged.

A gale off Finisterre scatters the ships, David Gwynn performs his exploit, and the first Channel engagements cost Spain dearly. Near Portland the English show superior seamanship in a general engagement. Motley pairs court paperwork with sea battle, showing how a grand design failed in the details of wind, supply, and command.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1588c:
John Lothrop Motley pauses his History of the United Netherlands in chapter nineteen to portrait Philip II in his cabinet. The king's system of work and deception governs empires from a desk. Spain and Italy wrote beautifully in that day, Motley notes. Philip's scrawl was like that of a clown just admitted to a writing school.

Across fifty-page despatches the royal margin carried a few awkward sentences, almost impossible to read. When deciphered, they revealed suggestions of astounding triviality. The most powerful man alive ruled by annotation, delay, and distrust of every servant. This famous character study explains the war's strange tempo: campaigns waited on one man's pen. Motley makes bureaucracy itself a tragic force, as fleets sail late because a king in the Escorial could not finish his paperwork.
uslaw-usc-t2-s168c: Section 168c of Title 2 of the United States Code covers printing and distribution of decennial editions and supplements to the Constitution Annotated. It sits in Chapter 5 of Title 2, on the Library of Congress, current through Public Law 119-134. The evidence shown is a closing clause of the provision. It states that the decennial revised edition and its cumulative pocket-part supplements shall be printed and distributed in one stated way. Both follow the provisions of any concurrent resolution adopted later on that subject.
uslaw-usc-t2-s288c:
Section 288c of Title 2 of the United States Code, in the chapter on the Office of Senate Legal Counsel, assigns that office the task of defending the Senate in court. When directed under the preceding section, the Counsel shall defend the Senate, its committees and subcommittees, and its Members, officers, and employees. The defense applies in civil actions in federal or state courts where they are made defendants.

The cases covered are those that put in issue the validity of a Senate proceeding or action taken in an official or representative capacity, including the issuance of a subpoena or order. The Counsel likewise defends the Senate side in proceedings about subpoenas or orders directed at them. A later part of the section deals with representation of a Member, officer, or employee in other settings.
uslaw-usc-t2-s28c:
Section 28c of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with sets of the Precedents. The Director of the Government Publishing Office hands the sets out. Each Member of the Ninety-fifth Congress is to get one set. Senators, House Members, Delegates, and the Resident Commissioner are all named.

The name of the Member must be stamped on each book's front cover. The stamp must be clear to read on the cover of each book. Members of later Congresses who lack a set may claim one too. They must send a writ request to the Superintendent of Documents. The next part of the section deals with more sets handed out. The rule made the Precedents a standard book on Members' shelves.
uslaw-usc-t2-s658c:
Section 658c of Title 2 of the United States Code sets the duties of the Director of the Congressional Budget Office on bills that carry federal mandates. It sits in the federal mandates part of the congressional budget chapter.

For each public bill or joint resolution reported by an authorizing committee, apart from spending bills, the Director must prepare a statement for the committee. Some bills place duties on state, local, or tribal governments. If the Director judges that the direct cost of those duties will reach fifty million dollars in the first year or any of the next four, the statement must say so plainly. It must give the estimate and briefly explain how the figure was reached. The estimates must also state the total direct cost of obeying the mandates in the bill.
